issues.legal_issue: The removal of an express debt-payment power from one provision does not eliminate the custodian’s power to pay evacuee debts when that power remains under the custodian’s general administration authority.
material_facts: An amendment removed the custodian’s express power to pay evacuee debts from one clause.
The custodian’s power to administer evacuee property and discharge evacuees’ obligations remained under other provisions.
issues.conclusion: The amendment did not impair the custodian’s power to pay evacuee debts, so it was unnecessary to decide whether the amendment was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 10(1) and 10(2)(n) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, the power to administer evacuee property includes the power to discharge obligations and pay debts the custodian considers binding. Raja Bhanupratap Singh v. Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property, U.P. was followed; it held that deleting the power from section 10(2)(m) did not affect the power arising under section 10(2)(n) read with section 10(1).

predicates.claim_against_evacuee_debtor: A creditor seeks payment of a debt owed by a person whose property is administered as evacuee property.
predicates.custodian_debt_administration_proceeding: The matter concerns the custodian’s administration of an evacuee debtor’s obligations.
predicates.custodian_retains_general_administration: The custodian continues to have authority to administer the debtor’s property.
predicates.custodian_can_discharge_evacuee_obligati: The custodian’s continuing authority includes discharging obligations binding on the debtor.

issues.definition: When a creditor’s claim concerns an evacuee debtor and the custodian retains authority both to administer the debtor’s property and to discharge the debtor’s obligations, the custodian retains power to pay evacuee debts.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of evacuee property does not violate a decree-holder’s right to acquire, hold, or dispose of property when the decree-holder has no proprietary interest in the acquired property.
material_facts: The appellant held decrees against evacuees but had no interest in the building that was acquired.
The building vested absolutely in the Central Government, free from encumbrances, after a notification was issued.
The appellant could no longer proceed against the building in execution of the decrees.
issues.conclusion: Section 12 did not interfere with the appellant’s property in the decrees, and the appellant could not rely on Article 19(1)(f) to challenge the acquisition of the building.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 extinguished the evacuees’ interests in property acquired by notification and vested that property in the Central Government free from encumbrances. Because the appellant had no interest in the building, the acquisition did not interfere with his right under Article 19(1)(f) to acquire, hold, and dispose of property; the Court therefore did not need to consider whether section 12 was saved by Article 19(5).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenges the constitutionality of a law or action that transfers property to the government.
predicates.decree_against_evacuee: The challenger holds a decree against a debtor whose property is treated as evacuee property.
predicates.acquired_asset_vested_in_government: The asset was transferred to and vested in the government through the acquisition process.
predicates.decree_holder_has_no_proprietary_interes: The decree-holder has a claim against the debtor but no ownership or other proprietary interest in the acquired asset.

issues.definition: When a decree-holder challenges an acquisition but has no proprietary interest in the asset that vested in government, the acquisition does not violate that decree-holder’s property right.

issues.legal_issue: A law that treats evacuee property differently from non-evacuee property does not violate equality when the classification has a rational connection to the law’s rehabilitation purpose.
material_facts: The acquisition law treated evacuee property differently from non-evacuee property.
The law was intended to use evacuee property in India for the rehabilitation of evacuees from Pakistan.
Creditors of evacuees could not execute against property after it vested in the Central Government, unlike creditors of non-evacuees.
issues.conclusion: The distinction between evacuee and non-evacuee property had a reasonable classification and a clear nexus with the rehabilitation purpose, so there was no violation of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require equality of all laws or their equal application to every person. Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 classified evacuee property separately, and its use for rehabilitation of evacuees from Pakistan was rationally connected to the object of the Act.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge: A person challenges different treatment of property under a law as unequal.
predicates.evacuee_property_treated_differently_fro: The law treats property associated with evacuees differently from other property.
predicates.distinction_advances_rehabilitation_purp: The different treatment is connected to using evacuee property to rehabilitate displaced evacuees.

issues.definition: When a law distinguishes evacuee property from other property and that distinction advances the rehabilitation of displaced evacuees, the classification does not violate equality.

issues.legal_issue: A law is not invalid merely because it impairs a contractual obligation when the Constitution contains no prohibition against such impairment.
material_facts: The appellant argued that acquisition of the debtor’s property impaired the debtors’ contractual obligation to him.
The appellant relied on decisions concerning a constitutional prohibition against laws impairing contractual obligations.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not invalidate the law on the ground that it impaired the contractual obligation because the Constitution contains no such prohibition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Von Hoffman v. City of Quincy, Ranger v. City of New Orleans, Peirce Coombes v. Milton E. Getz, and W. B. Worthen Co. v. Thomas, which concerned a prohibition in the United States Constitution against laws impairing contractual obligations. The Indian Constitution contains no equivalent prohibition.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_based_on_contra: A person challenges a law on the ground that it impairs a contractual obligation owed to that person.
predicates.challenged_law_affects_contractual_oblig: The law changes the practical effect or enforceability of a contractual obligation.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge rests on the effect of a law on a contractual obligation, that impairment alone does not invalidate the law.

issues.legal_issue: A creditor whose execution against acquired evacuee property is barred may ask the custodian to consider payment from funds held when the property vested, if the creditor establishes that the property belonged to the debtor and satisfies the custodian’s requirements.
material_facts: The appellant could not proceed against the building or its income after the building vested in the Central Government.
The appellant alleged that release deeds in favour of the judgment-debtors’ wives were fictitious and fraudulent and that the property therefore belonged to the judgment-debtors.
The Court directed the trial court to decide the release-deed issue and observed that, if the appellant succeeded, he could approach the custodian concerning any money held on the date of vesting.
The custodian’s decision whether to pay remained subject to the applicable requirements and the custodian’s judgment.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not proceed against the building or its income after vesting, but if the trial court found in his favour on the release deeds, he could ask the custodian to make such orders as the custodian considered appropriate concerning money held at vesting.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 10(1) and 10(2)(n) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 permit the custodian to consider paying a debt from funds under the custodian’s control. Under Raja Bhanupratap Singh v. Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property, U.P., a civil decree does not itself determine entitlement to payment; the custodian determines whether the claimant is entitled. The Court directed the trial court to decide whether the release deeds were fictitious and fraudulent and held that a favourable finding would permit the appellant to approach the custodian, not guarantee payment.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenging_transfer_as_fraudulent and creditor_claim_against_evacuee_debtor and property_vested_in_government and funds_held_by_custodian_at_vesting and trial_finds_property_belonged_to_debtor

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_transfer_as_fraud: A creditor brings a civil suit alleging that a transfer of the debtor’s property was fictitious or intended to defeat creditors.
predicates.creditor_claim_against_evacuee_debtor: The claimant seeks satisfaction of a debt owed by a person whose property is administered as evacuee property.
predicates.property_vested_in_government: The property at issue vested in the government through acquisition.
predicates.funds_held_by_custodian_at_vesting: The custodian held money associated with the property when it vested in the government.
predicates.trial_finds_property_belonged_to_debtor: The trial court determines that the disputed property belonged to the debtor rather than to the transferee.

issues.definition: When a creditor challenges a transfer as fraudulent, the property vests in government, the custodian holds associated funds, and the trial court finds the property belonged to the debtor, the creditor may apply to the custodian for payment.
